before: Agreeable to this are all those plain declarations of Saint John in his first epistle. Hereby we know that we know him, if we keep his commandments. 1 John 2:3. Whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. Hereby we know that we are in him, that we are indeed the children of God. 1 John 2:5.

If you know that he is righteous, you know that everyone who does righteousness is born of him. 1 John 2:29. We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers. 1 John 3:4. Hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him. 1 John 3:18. That is because we love one another, not in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and in truth.
Hereby we know that we dwell in him, because he has given us of his loving Spirit. 1 John 4:13. And hereby we know that he abides in us, by the obedient Spirit which he has given us. 1 John 3:24.

before: In the same verse also, in which he calls this, the way of love, a more excellent way, he directs the Corinthians to desire other gifts besides it, yes, to desire them earnestly. Earnestly desire, he says, the best gifts, and yet I show you a more excellent way (1 Corinthians 12:31). More excellent than what? Than the gifts of healing, of speaking with tongues (1 Corinthians 12:28), and of interpreting, mentioned in the preceding verse. But not more excellent than the way of obedience. Of this the apostle is not speaking. Neither is he speaking of outward religion at all. So that this text is quite wide of the present question.

before: If any man marvels at this, let him acknowledge he is a stranger to the whole religion of Jesus Christ: and in particular, to that perfect portraiture of it, which he has set before us in this discourse. For how far short is all this, of that righteousness and true holiness, which he has described in it! how widely distant from that inward kingdom of heaven, which is now opened in the believing soul? Which is first sown in the heart as a grain of mustard-seed (Matthew 17:20), but afterwards puts forth great branches, on which grow all the fruits of righteousness, every good temper and word and work.

before: Yes, say some, but God has appointed another way. Stand still, and see the salvation of God.
Let us examine the scriptures to which you refer. The first of them, with the context, runs thus.

And when Pharaoh drew near, the children of Israel lifted up their eyes, and they were sorely afraid. And they said to Moses, Because there were no graves in Egypt, have you taken us away to die in the wilderness? And Moses said to the people, Do not fear. Stand still, and see the salvation of the Lord. And the Lord said to Moses, Speak to the children of Israel, that they go forward. But lift up your rod, and stretch out your hand over the sea, and divide it. And the children of Israel shall go on dry ground through the midst of the sea. Exodus 14:10.
This was the salvation of God which they stood still to see, by marching forward with all their might.

The other passage in which this expression occurs stands thus. There came some who told Jehoshaphat, saying, There comes a great multitude against you, from beyond the sea. And Jehoshaphat feared, and set himself to seek the Lord, and proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah. And Judah gathered themselves together to ask help of the Lord. Out of all the cities they came to seek the Lord. And Jehoshaphat stood in the congregation, in the house of the Lord. Then upon Jahaziel came the Spirit of the Lord. And he said, Do not be dismayed by reason of this great multitude. Tomorrow go down against them. You shall not need to fight in this battle. Set yourselves. Stand still, and see the salvation of the Lord. And they arose early in the morning and went forth. And when they began to sing and to praise, the Lord set ambushes against the children of Moab, Ammon, and Mount Seir, and everyone helped to destroy another. 2 Chronicles 20:2.
Such was the salvation which the children of Judah saw. But how does all this prove that we ought not to wait for the grace of God in the means which he has ordained?

before: And in this sense also, "everyone who loves him who begat, loves him who is begotten of him" (1 John 5:1). His spirit rejoices in God his Savior (Luke 1:47). He loves the Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity (Ephesians 6:24). He is so joined to the Lord as to be one spirit (1 Corinthians 6:17). His soul hangs upon him, and chooses him as altogether lovely (Song of Solomon 5:16), the chief among ten thousand (Song of Solomon 5:10). He knows, he feels, what that means: "My beloved is mine, and I am his" (Song of Solomon 2:16). "You are fairer than the children of men (Psalm 45:2). Full of grace are your lips, because God has anointed you forever" (Psalm 45:7).

before: He also spoke another parable, to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint, until through this means they should receive from God whatever petition they asked of him.

There was in a city a judge who did not fear God, and did not regard man. And there was a widow in that city, and she came to him, saying, Avenge me of my adversary. And he would not for a while. But afterward he said within himself, Though I do not fear God, nor regard man, yet because this widow troubles me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me. Luke 18:1-4.

Our Lord himself has made the application of this. Hear what the unjust judge says. Because she continues to ask, because she will take no denial, therefore I will avenge her. And shall not God avenge his own elect, who cry day and night to him? I tell you, he will avenge them speedily, if they pray and do not faint.

before: The very first sermon of St. Paul’s, which is recorded, concludes in these words. By him all that believe are justified from all things, from which they could not be justified by the law of Moses. Beware therefore lest that come upon you which is spoken of in the Prophets, Behold you despisers and wonder and perish (Acts 13:41). For I work a work in your days, a work which you will in no wise believe, though a man declare it to you, (Acts 13:39). Now it is manifest, all this is preaching the law, in the sense wherein you understand the term: even although great part of, if not all his hearers, were either Jews or religious proselytes, (Acts 13:43), and therefore probably many of them, in some degree at least, convinced of sin already. He first reminds them, That they could not be justified by the law of Moses, but only by faith in Christ: and then severely threatens them with the judgments of God, which is in the strongest sense preaching the law.

before: These blasphemers might almost persuade those to imagine themselves guiltless who, in the contrary extreme, hope to fulfill the commands of God without taking any pains at all. Vain hope! That a child of Adam should ever expect to see the kingdom of Christ and of God without striving, without agonizing first to enter in at the strait gate (Matthew 7:13). That one who was conceived and born in sin (Psalm 51:5), and whose inward parts are very wickedness, should once entertain a thought of being purified as his Lord is pure, unless he treads in his steps and takes up his cross daily (Luke 9:23); unless he cuts off his right hand, and plucks out the right eye (Matthew 5:29-30) and casts it from him. That he should ever dream of shaking off his old opinions, passions, and tempers, of being sanctified throughout in spirit, soul, and body (1 Thessalonians 5:23), without a constant and continued course of general self-denial.

before: Behold Christianity in its native form, as delivered by its great Author. This is the genuine religion of Jesus Christ. Such he presents it to the one whose eyes are opened. See a picture of God, so far as he can be imitated by a person. A picture drawn by God's own hand. Behold, you despisers, and wonder, and perish (Acts 13:41). Or rather, wonder and adore. Rather cry out, Is this the religion of Jesus of Nazareth, the religion which I persecuted? Let me no more be found even fighting against God (Acts 5:39). Lord, what would you have me do (Acts 9:6)? What beauty appears in the whole. How just a symmetry. What exact proportion in every part. How desirable is the happiness described here. How venerable, how lovely the holiness. This is the spirit of religion, the very essence of it. These are indeed the fundamentals of Christianity. Oh, that we may not be hearers of it only (James 1:22), like a person looking at his own face in a mirror (James 1:23), who goes away and immediately forgets what kind of person he was. No. Let us look steadily into this perfect law of liberty (James 1:25), and continue in it. Let us not rest until every line of it is copied into our own hearts. Let us watch, and pray, and believe, and love, and strive for the mastery, until every part of it appears in our soul, engraved there by the finger of God, until we are holy as he who has called us is holy (1 Peter 1:16), perfect as our Father who is in heaven is perfect (Matthew 5:48).
